title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 314
paragraphs: Up to this point my own observation, judgment, and inquiry are the vouchers for what I have said; but from this point onwards I am about to tell the history of Egypt according to what I heard, to which will be added something of what I have myself seen.

Of Min, who first became king of Egypt, the priests said that he banked off the site of Memphis from the river; for the whole stream of the river used to flow along the sandy mountain-range on the side of Libya, but Min formed, by embankments, that bend of the river which lies to the south about a hundred furlongs above Memphis, and thus he dried up the old stream and led the river so that it flowed in the middle between the mountains. Even now this bend of the Nile is kept by the Persians under very careful watch, that it may flow in the channel to which it is confined, and the bank is repaired every year; for if the river should break through and overflow in this direction, Memphis would be in danger of being overwhelmed by flood. When this Min, who first became king, had turned into dry land the part that was dammed off, he founded in it that city which is now called Memphis (for Memphis too is in the narrow part of Egypt); and outside the city he dug round it to the north and west a lake communicating with the river, since the east side is barred by the Nile itself. Secondly, he established in the city the temple of Hephaestus, a great work and most worthy of mention.
